metadata.title: The 10% Life
metadata.description: The Art of Return: Strategic Wilderness Integration

slides.title: You've been running at 100%.
slides.content: And calling it living. Success was supposed to be the finish line, not just the beginning of a race we never chose.
slides.notes: Hold up the mirror. Name the exhaustion of the urban trap. The average professional spends less than 2% outdoors.
slides.narrationText:
You’ve been running at full tilt for so long that it starts to feel normal. That’s the trap... success becomes the finish line, and then, quietly, it turns into another race you never actually agreed to run. uhm, and somewhere in that loop, less than 2% of your time is spent outdoors.

That number matters because it tells the truth about what modern life has done to us. Most of your days are spent inside systems, inside screens, inside other people’s deadlines. The body adapts, sure, but it doesn’t forget. It keeps asking for air, light, movement, silence... and most of us keep answering with more output. Well, that’s not living at 100%. That’s just maintaining pressure.

See, the exhaustion isn’t only physical. It’s the constant state of readiness, the sense that if you stop, things slip. You learn to call that ambition. You learn to call that discipline. But after a while, it becomes hard to tell the difference between momentum and depletion. And the strange part is, the more successful you become, the easier it is to normalize the strain.

That matters because what you protect shapes everything else. If 98% of your year is spent in the machine, then your mind, your attention, your relationships... they all start to move like the machine. So the real question isn’t whether you can keep going. It’s what happens if you stop pretending that this pace is sustainable.

And once you see that clearly... the next question is obvious: what does it look like to protect just a fraction of the year, on purpose?

slides.title: What if 90% was enough?
slides.content: 30 nights a year in the deep quiet of the wilderness. Enough time to reset your circadian rhythm. Not subtraction — protection.
slides.notes: Explain the 10% solution: 30 nights annually. A practice, not a holiday. The math of transformation.
slides.narrationText:
That’s the point... 90% is often where your life starts working again. Thirty nights a year is not a retreat from real life, uhm, it’s protection for the part of you that has to keep showing up.

See, the math here is quiet but it changes everything. You’re not trying to live in the forest full-time. You’re creating a rhythm that interrupts the blur before it hardens into a way of being. Thirty nights across a year gives your body repeated contact with deep quiet, with dark enough skies, with mornings that don’t begin in a car or a meeting. That’s how circadian rhythm gets reset — not by one dramatic reset, but by returning often enough that your system remembers what normal feels like. And no, this isn’t subtraction. It’s not taking away from your life in the city. It’s protecting a fraction of the year so the rest of it doesn’t get eaten alive by pace.

Right, and that matters because exhaustion rarely announces itself cleanly. It shows up as shorter patience, thinner attention, that strange sense that even good days feel slightly overdrawn. Protect 10% of your year, and the other 90% stops being a grind you survive and starts becoming something you can actually inhabit.

So the question isn’t whether you need a long break once. The question is whether your year has a pulse. And if it does... what would a decade of that protection change?

slides.title: Seven years of quiet work.
slides.content: 6 collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. We didn't just find land — we restore it. Earn trust with substance.
slides.notes: Six collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. Seven years. Each number as its own sentence. Regeneration, not development.
slides.narrationText:
Seven years is long enough to fake a story, and still not long enough to hold one together. uhm… this one holds because the work is visible in the ground, not just in the language.

Six collectives. 1,300 acres. 250 families. Those numbers don’t sit there as decoration. They tell you this is not a single beautiful place with a narrative wrapped around it. It is a system, spread across different landscapes, with real people inside it, returning to it, depending on it. Six collectives means six separate places learning how to live with land instead of extracting from it. 1,300 acres means the work has scale, but not the glossy kind. The slow kind. The kind that takes years of soil, water, canopy, and trust. And 250 families means this is already social, already lived in, already carrying responsibility beyond the founders. Well… that matters.

We didn’t just find land — we restore it. That line carries the whole difference. Finding land is easy. Restoring it means degraded ground, patient repair, and a willingness to stay when the work is not photogenic. Earn trust with substance. That is the real proof here. Not marketing proof. Field proof.

And the implication is simple: if you’re going to protect 10% of your year, it has to be inside something real. Not an idea. Not a mood. A place that has already been tested by weather, season, and time. Something you can return to without wondering whether it will still be there in the same way.

That’s why the next question isn’t whether this sounds nice... it’s what it actually feels like to belong here.

slides.title: Rewilded landscapes by Beforest.
slides.content: Poomaale 1.0 & 2.0, Coorg · Hammiyala, Coorg · Hyderabad · Bhopal · Mumbai. Belonging to a place, not just visiting.
slides.notes: Showcase the sanctuaries. Ancient forests, coffee plantations, grasslands. Not amenities — transformation.
slides.narrationText:
This is where it stops being an idea and starts becoming a place. Uhm... not a concept, not a brochure, a place with canopy, soil, weather, and a rhythm that keeps going after you leave.

Poomaale in Coorg is ancient forest and coffee. Hammiyala is coffee agroforestry and grassland at altitude. Hyderabad holds the Deccan edge — rocks, scrub, a different kind of silence. Bhopal sits in the Central Highlands, where the land opens differently. Mumbai... well, Mumbai is the closest thing to chaos we know, and that matters too. These aren’t properties arranged for convenience. They’re rewilded landscapes, each one shaped by what the land already is, and by what it can become when it’s restored instead of replaced.

See, the point isn’t that each collective gives you a beautiful place to stay. The point is that each one changes your relationship with where you land. You don’t arrive as a consumer of scenery. You arrive into a living system that has been brought back to itself. That does something to you. It slows the nervous system down. It sharpens attention. It makes belonging feel less abstract and more physical.

And that matters because exhaustion isn’t just about work. It’s about never having a place that asks you to recalibrate. Uhm... these landscapes do that quietly. They don’t entertain you. They hold you long enough for you to feel the difference.

That’s the real shift here. Not a collection of escapes. A set of places where belonging is practiced. And once you see that, the question becomes... what does access to that kind of life actually look like?

slides.title: 300 Nights of Intentional Living.
slides.content: 30 person-nights per year for 10 years. Across all Beforest Collectives. Access, not ownership. No carry-forward — rhythm, not accumulation.
slides.notes: Address objections directly. Person-nights, not family nights. Frame it as a recurring reset practice.
slides.narrationText:
And that rhythm only works if the structure is clean. Thirty person-nights a year. Ten years. Across all Beforest Collectives. Uhm... that part matters more than it looks.

Because this isn’t a cabin you keep returning to out of habit, and it isn’t a family package you stretch and bend until the meaning disappears. It’s person-nights, which means the unit is the individual practice. Your immediate family can come in, yes — but the membership itself is built around your own reset, your own calendar, your own return. Children under 12 don’t count toward person-nights, which keeps the shape humane. And there’s no carry-forward, because the point is not to stockpile nights like credits. The point is to protect a rhythm that keeps showing up through the decade.

Right, that’s the real distinction here. Access, not ownership. You don’t own land. You own the right to enter a living system that Beforest restores and operates. That changes the psychology completely. You stop treating nature like an occasional reward and start treating it like a standing practice... something that sits in the year and quietly steadies everything else.

And uhm, once you see it that way, the objections change shape. It stops being about squeezing more into one trip. It becomes about whether you want a repeatable reset built into your life, or another thing you’ll mean to do later.

That’s why the next question is simple: if the practice is clear, what does it feel like when you actually step into it?

slides.title: The weight of 'Next Year'.
slides.content: Every year you wait is a year of 10% you don't get back. This isn't about missing an opportunity; it's about missing a version of yourself.
slides.notes: Move away from sales urgency. Focus on the personal cost of waiting. Calibration and reset are needed now, not eventually.
slides.narrationText:
And that’s the part people don’t say out loud... next year is never neutral. It doesn’t just pass. It takes a year of your 10% with it, and you don’t get that rhythm back.

Well, the real loss isn’t the booking window or the price moving on. It’s the version of you that stays in the same pattern for another twelve months. The one that keeps saying “later” to rest, to recalibration, to a slower kind of intelligence. Uhm, that sounds abstract until you’ve lived a few years of it — the body knows. The mind starts normalizing strain. The calendar gets full, and suddenly the idea of protecting ten percent of your year feels unusual, when it should feel basic. This is why the offer is framed as a practice across a decade, not a one-time indulgence. Thirty nights a year is not about collecting nights. It’s about building a return path to yourself, again and again, before the year hardens into habit. And no, wait... that’s the quiet cost here: time spent without a reset becomes a kind of drift.

So the consequence is simple. If you keep postponing the reset, the fatigue doesn’t stay put — it compounds. Your work gets sharper only up to a point, and then it starts borrowing from your sleep, your patience, your relationships. Protecting 10% now changes the rest of the year in ways you only notice after you’ve done it.

And that’s why the next question isn’t whether this sounds good. It’s whether you want to feel it once, properly, before deciding.

slides.title: Blyton Bungalow: The First 1%.
slides.content: Experience before commitment. A Kodava-inspired sanctuary built from the earth. 128 acres of private coffee forest in Coorg.
slides.notes: Details: Hospitality without the footprint. 6 signature rooms. 60 million liters of water conserved. 90-point coffee. The pilot, not the backup plan. Every rupee of the trial stay adjusts toward membership.
slides.narrationText:
This is where it stops being an idea and becomes a place you can actually stand in. Blyton Bungalow is the first 1% because it asks for something simple... come once, feel the ground, and let the land answer for itself.

A Kodava-inspired sanctuary built from the earth, inside 128 acres of private coffee forest in Coorg. Six signature rooms. Not a big resort, not a performance of abundance — just enough structure for the forest to stay dominant. The numbers matter here: 60 million liters of water conserved, a 90-point coffee, and hospitality that leaves almost no footprint behind. That is not decoration. That is the discipline of making comfort without taking more than you should.

See, this is what “experience before commitment” really means. You are not being asked to trust a brochure or a promise... uhm, you are being asked to spend time in a living system and notice what changes in you. The trial stay is the pilot, not the backup plan. It is the first honest contact with a way of living that already exists, already works, and already has a shape.

And if it lands, the amount you spend there adjusts toward membership. So the visit is not separate from the decision — it is part of it. That matters because certainty is hard to get from words alone. You only really know when your body has been in the room, when the forest has changed the pace of your breathing.

So go once. Let the place do its work... then decide whether you want 300 nights of this, held across ten years. You decide with your feet, not your eyes. See you in the slow lane.
